messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Multivariate with differently distributed observations
parts:
Hi folks,

I could't find anything on this topic in the manual nor in the groups, but possibly my search was not sufficient. I'm curious if it's possible to simultaneously model two DVs that have different distributions; say one is a binomial variable and the other is continuous and assumed to have Gaussian error. As a specific example, consider data from a simple psychology experiment where multiple human participants are asked to perform some simple 2-alternative perceptual discrimination as quickly as possible across a few hundred trials. For each trial and each participant, we observe two pieces of data: how fast the response was made and whether it is accurate or not. To simplify, let's assume that there is no trial-by-trial correlation between response times (RTs) and error rates (ERs), and also that RTs have a fixed trial-by-trial Gaussian error of 100ms.

One might be interested in a model that samples each participant's deviation for each DV from that DV's population mean from a bivariate normal with estimable correlation matrix, accounting for the possibility that faster participants are more error prone, for example. But I'm not sure whether stan is set up to return sensible results when the log-probability is being updated by two differently-scaled DVs like this. My imagined model would be something like:

    data{ 
        int<lower=0> unit_count ;
        int<lower=0> row_count ;
        int<lower=0> unit[row_count] ; 
        int<lower=0,upper=1> er[row_count] ;
        real<lower=0> rt[row_count] ;
    }
    transformed data{
        vector[2] zero_vector ; // dummy parameter to employ the Matt trick for multivariate models
        for (k in 1:2) {
            zero_vector[k] <- 0 ; // filling the zero vector
        }
    }
    parameters {
        real unit_logit_er_mean ;
        real<lower=0> unit_logit_er_sd ;
        real unit_rt_mean ;
        real<lower=0> unit_rt_sd ;
        corr_matrix[2] cors ;
        vector[2] betas[unit_count] ; // dummy parameter to employ the matt trick.
    }
    transformed parameters {
        //using Matt trick here
        vector[unit_count] unit_logit_er ;
        vector[unit_count] unit_rt ;
        for(this_unit in 1:unit_count){
            unit_logit_er[this_unit] <- unit_logit_er_mean + betas[this_unit,1]*unit_logit_er_sd ;
            unit_rt[this_unit] <- unit_rt_mean + betas[this_unit,2]*unit_rt_sd ;
        }
    }
    model {  
        //set priors on population parameters
        unit_logit_er_mean ~ normal(-3,1) ;
        unit_logit_er_sd ~ cauchy(0,2) ;
        unit_rt_mean ~ normal(300,50) ;
        unit_rt_sd ~ normal(200,10) ;
        
        //set prior on correlation matrix
        cors ~ lkj_corr(2) ;
        
        //define multivariate sampling of unit-specific parameters (using Matt Trick ; see transformed parameters)
        for (this_unit in 1:unit_count){
            betas[this_unit] ~ multi_normal(zero_vector,cors) ;
        }
        
        //iterate over trials and increment log-probability
        for(row in 1:row_count){
            increment_log_prob(binomial_logit_log(er[row],1,unit_logit_er[unit[row]])) ;
            increment_log_prob(normal_log(rt[row],1,unit_rt[unit[row]],100)) ;
        }
    } 

Would stan treat this sensibly? Or is this a malformed model from stan's perspective?

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Multivariate with differently distributed observations
parts:
That makes a lot of sense and I have no idea why I haven't seen
more models like this --- it makes a lot of sense.

I don't see any reason it wouldn't work in Stan. As
long as the densities make sense, Stan should be OK.

The best thing to do, as usual, is to simulate data from
the model (or ideally a simpler one) to test whether you
can fit the model you have in mind (or use the technique
you have in mind).

- Bob

P.S. Out of curiousity, what does "DV" stand for?
